sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation [MATH: \dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1]

are given by [MATH: x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t},]

where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at [MATH: (0, \pm a).] From the graph, we have that [MATH: (0,9)] is a vertex of the hyperbola, so [MATH: a=9.]

The asymptotes of a vertical hyperbola are [MATH: y = \pm \dfrac{a}{b}x.] In our case, the asymptotes are [MATH: y = \pm 3 x,] and so we have

[MATH: (a)/(b)|= 3; (9)/(b)|= 3; b|= 3.]

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are [MATH: x=3\tan{t},\quad y=9\sec{t}.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
We've used the fact that the parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin are

Content:
[MATH: x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t}.]

Content:
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are positive constants. Now, we'll demonstrate why this is true.

Content:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

Content:
[MATH: x|= b\tan t|⟹|\tan t|= (x)/(b),; y|= a\sec t|⟹|\sec t|= (y)/(a).]

Content:
Now, we recall the secant-tangent identity:

Content:
[MATH: \tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}.]

Content:
Substituting the above into the secant-tangent identity, we get

Content:
[MATH: \tan^{2} t + 1|= \sec^{2} t; ((x)/(b))^{2} + 1|= ((y)/(a))^{2}; (x^{2})/(b^{2}) + 1|= (y^{2})/(a^{2}); (y^{2})/(a^{2}) − (x^{2})/(b^{2})|= 1.]

Content:
This is the Cartesian equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin. Therefore, the parametric equations do indeed describe a vertical hyperbola.

items.title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations

key_prerequisites.name: Simplifying Expressions Using the Secant-Tangent Identity

sections.normalized_html: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola [MATH: x =2\tan{t}, \, y =3\sec{t}.]
sections.readable_text: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola [MATH: x =2\tan{t}, \, y =3\sec{t}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter [MATH: t.] We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

  • Isolating the [MATH: \tan{t}] term in the [MATH: x]-equation and squaring, we get [MATH: x|= 2\tan t; (x)/(2)|= \tan t; (x^{2})/(2^{2})|= \tan^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4)|= \tan^{2} t.]

  • Isolating the [MATH: \sec{t}] term in the [MATH: y]-equation and squaring, we get [MATH: y|= 3\sec t; (y)/(3)|= \sec t; (y^{2})/(3^{2})|= \sec^{2} t; (y^{2})/(9)|= \sec^{2} t.]

Substituting the two equations into the identity [MATH: \tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}] and rearranging, we get [MATH: \tan^{2} t + 1|= \sec^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4) + 1|= (y^{2})/(9); (y^{2})/(9) − (x^{2})/(4)|= 1.]
sections.readable_text:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter [MATH: t.] We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the [MATH: \tan{t}] term in the [MATH: x]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: x|= 2\tan t; (x)/(2)|= \tan t; (x^{2})/(2^{2})|= \tan^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4)|= \tan^{2} t.]
- Isolating the [MATH: \sec{t}] term in the [MATH: y]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: y|= 3\sec t; (y)/(3)|= \sec t; (y^{2})/(3^{2})|= \sec^{2} t; (y^{2})/(9)|= \sec^{2} t.]

Substituting the two equations into the identity [MATH: \tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}] and rearranging, we get
[MATH: \tan^{2} t + 1|= \sec^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4) + 1|= (y^{2})/(9); (y^{2})/(9) − (x^{2})/(4)|= 1.]

Example Prompt:
Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola [MATH: x =2\tan{t}, \, y =3\sec{t}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter [MATH: t.] We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the [MATH: \tan{t}] term in the [MATH: x]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: x|= 2\tan t; (x)/(2)|= \tan t; (x^{2})/(2^{2})|= \tan^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4)|= \tan^{2} t.]
- Isolating the [MATH: \sec{t}] term in the [MATH: y]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: y|= 3\sec t; (y)/(3)|= \sec t; (y^{2})/(3^{2})|= \sec^{2} t; (y^{2})/(9)|= \sec^{2} t.]

Substituting the two equations into the identity [MATH: \tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}] and rearranging, we get
[MATH: \tan^{2} t + 1|= \sec^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4) + 1|= (y^{2})/(9); (y^{2})/(9) − (x^{2})/(4)|= 1.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1]

Content:
are given by

Content:
[MATH: x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t},]

Content:
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants. The domain of the parameter [MATH: t] is

Content:
[MATH: t\in[-\pi,\pi],\qquad t\neq \pm \frac{\pi}{2}.]

Content:
The branches corresponding to different values of [MATH: t] are shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/af5df25094578ebacde5afd40c5acff1]

Content:
This parametrization contains discontinuities at [MATH: t=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}.] One consequence of this is that the curve appears to "jump" between different quadrants at the singular points.

Content:
For the most part, we won't worry too much about the domain of [MATH: t.] However, it does become important when we're parametrizing part of a hyperbola, which we'll deal with later.

Content:
Note: To understand where this parametrization comes from, recall the trigonometric identity
[MATH: 1 + \tan^2 t = \sec^2 t.]
Rearranging, we get
[MATH: \sec^2 t - \tan^2 t =1,]
which means
[MATH: \sec^{2} t|= (y^{2})/(a^{2})⇒y = a\sec t; \tan^{2} t|= (x^{2})/(b^{2})⇒x = b\tan t.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Vertical Hyperbola Given Algebraically

Example Prompt:
What are the parametric equations of the hyperbola [MATH: \dfrac{y^2}{9} - \dfrac{x^2}{25} = 1?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation
[MATH: \frac{y^2}{a^2} - \frac{x^2}{b^2} = 1]
are given by
[MATH: x = b\tan{t}, \quad y = a\sec{t}.]
In our case, [MATH: a = \sqrt{9} = 3] and [MATH: b = \sqrt{25} = 5.] Therefore, the parametric equations are
[MATH: x = 5\tan{t}, \quad y = 3\sec{t}.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Vertical Hyperbola Given Graphically

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/8c6c7cf5762a3078063987d1dc5eb95f]

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are [MATH: y=\pm 3x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation
[MATH: \dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1]

are given by
[MATH: x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t},]

where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at [MATH: (0, \pm a).] From the graph, we have that [MATH: (0,9)] is a vertex of the hyperbola, so [MATH: a=9.]

The asymptotes of a vertical hyperbola are [MATH: y = \pm \dfrac{a}{b}x.] In our case, the asymptotes are [MATH: y = \pm 3 x,] and so we have

[MATH: (a)/(b)|= 3; (9)/(b)|= 3; b|= 3.]

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are
[MATH: x=3\tan{t},\quad y=9\sec{t}.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Proof That the Parametric Equations Describe a Vertical Hyperbola

Content:
We've used the fact that the parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin are

Content:
[MATH: x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t}.]

Content:
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are positive constants. Now, we'll demonstrate why this is true.

Content:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

Content:
[MATH: x|= b\tan t|⟹|\tan t|= (x)/(b),; y|= a\sec t|⟹|\sec t|= (y)/(a).]

Content:
Now, we recall the secant-tangent identity:

Content:
[MATH: \tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}.]

Content:
Substituting the above into the secant-tangent identity, we get

Content:
[MATH: \tan^{2} t + 1|= \sec^{2} t; ((x)/(b))^{2} + 1|= ((y)/(a))^{2}; (x^{2})/(b^{2}) + 1|= (y^{2})/(a^{2}); (y^{2})/(a^{2}) − (x^{2})/(b^{2})|= 1.]

Content:
This is the Cartesian equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin. Therefore, the parametric equations do indeed describe a vertical hyperbola.

---

Item 9 — Example: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations

Example Prompt:
Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola [MATH: x =2\tan{t}, \, y =3\sec{t}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter [MATH: t.] We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the [MATH: \tan{t}] term in the [MATH: x]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: x|= 2\tan t; (x)/(2)|= \tan t; (x^{2})/(2^{2})|= \tan^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4)|= \tan^{2} t.]
- Isolating the [MATH: \sec{t}] term in the [MATH: y]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: y|= 3\sec t; (y)/(3)|= \sec t; (y^{2})/(3^{2})|= \sec^{2} t; (y^{2})/(9)|= \sec^{2} t.]

Substituting the two equations into the identity [MATH: \tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}] and rearranging, we get
[MATH: \tan^{2} t + 1|= \sec^{2} t; (x^{2})/(4) + 1|= (y^{2})/(9); (y^{2})/(9) − (x^{2})/(4)|= 1.]

Item 12 — Example: Parametrizing Part of a Vertical Hyperbola

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/b31abfb21d7c23e3c4f5c2a1ed1eb344]

The quarter-hyperbola above is defined by the parametric equations

[MATH: x = \sqrt3\tan{t}, \qquad y = \sqrt2\sec{t}.]

What is the domain of the parameter [MATH: t?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

[MATH: x= \sqrt3 \tan{t}, \quad
y = \sqrt2 \sec{t}, \quad
t \in [-\pi,\pi], \quad
t \neq \pm\dfrac{\pi}2.]

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-hyperbola, we refer to the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/ff70cc02658a737d406109329d5c2ccf]

We can see that if we restrict [MATH: t] to [MATH: \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right]] we get the required quarter-hyperbola.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe the required quarter-hyperbola are

[MATH: x= \sqrt3\tan{t}, \quad
y = \sqrt2\sec{t}, \quad
t \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}2,0\right].]
